steps.title: Aggregate to user-level
steps.description: Aggregate session-level data to user-level since variant is assigned per user, computing user conversion (any session converted) and averaging platform/day covariates.

options.label: User converted if any session converted
options.rationale: Define user-level conversion as 1 if any of their sessions resulted in a purchase, reflecting user-level decision.
options.spec: Group by user_id. For each user: compute user_converted = max(converted) across sessions; user_treatment = variant of first session (all same per user); user_platform = mode of platform; user_day_mean = mean of day; return dataframe with one row per user and columns: user_id, user_converted, user_treatment, user_platform, user_day_mean.

options.label: User conversion proportion
options.rationale: Use the proportion of sessions converted per user as a more granular outcome, especially for users with multiple sessions.

options.label: Unadjusted
options.rationale: Estimate the raw treatment effect without covariate adjustment; valid due to randomization but less precise.

options.rationale: Adjust for platform (web, iOS, Android) to account for known differences in conversion behavior across devices.

steps.title: Estimate conversion lift
steps.description: Estimate the treatment effect on user-level conversion using different statistical approaches for the same estimand.

options.label: OLS linear regression
options.rationale: Fit an ordinary least squares model with user_converted as the outcome to estimate the absolute probability lift (treatment - control) in percentage points.
options.spec: Fit an OLS regression (statsmodels.api.OLS) of user_converted on user_treatment (dummy coded: treatment=1, control=0) and covariates indicated by ctx['covariates'] (with platform dropped first if present). Use HC1 (heteroskedasticity-consistent) standard errors. Return the coefficient for user_treatment as estimate (in percentage points, so multiply by 100), its 95% CI, and p-value.

options.label: Logistic regression GLM
options.rationale: Fit a logistic regression model to estimate the log-odds effect, then convert to average marginal effect in percentage points for comparability with the linear probability model.
options.spec: Fit a GLM with binomial family and logit link (statsmodels.api.GLM) of user_converted on user_treatment (treatment=1, control=0) and covariates in ctx['covariates'] (platform dropped first if present). Obtain the average marginal effect of user_treatment using statsmodels.discrete.discrete_margins.AverageMarginalEffects, representing the average change in predicted probability (treatment - control) in probability units. Multiply by 100 for percentage points. Use model-based standard errors for the marginal effect to compute 95% CI and p-value.

data.reason: Excluding internal/test sessions improves validity by removing non-customer activity; common practice in A/B testing.

Changing the outcome from binary conversion to continuous proportion alters the interpretation of the effect and deviates from the specified estimand (difference in conversion rates). This requires justification beyond convenience.
Unadjusted analysis is acceptable under randomization, though less precise than adjusting for known prognostic covariates like platform.

Adjusting for both platform and user-level average day controls for known confounders (device type and temporal trends) without leaking outcome information; this is a reasonable extension of the conventional platform-only adjustment.
Logistic regression with average marginal effects is a well-established alternative to LPM for binary outcomes, providing comparable estimates while respecting the bounded nature of probabilities.
Excluding bot-like sessions via a duration threshold improves data quality by removing noise unlikely to represent real user behavior; this is a common preprocessing step in online experiments.

Excluding internal and bot-like sessions improves measurement of genuine customer behavior without changing the estimand, assuming such exclusions do not introduce bias by being related to treatment assignment.

options.spec: Group by user_id. For each user: compute user_converted = max(converted) across sessions; user_treatment = variant of first session (all same per user); user_platform = mode of platform; user_day_mean = mean of day; return dataframe with one row per user and columns: user_id, user_converted, user_treatment, user_platform, user_day_mean.
options.code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def apply(df, ctx):
    # user_converted: 1 if any session converted
    user_converted = df.groupby("user_id")["converted"].max().reset_index()["converted"]
    # user_treatment: variant of first session (all same per user)
    user_treatment = df.groupby("user_id")["variant"].first().reset_index()["variant"]
    # user_platform: mode of platform per user
    user_platform = df.groupby("user_id")["platform"].apply(lambda x: x.mode().iloc[0] if not x.mode().empty else np.nan).reset_index()["platform"]
    # user_day_mean: mean of day per user
    user_day_mean = df.groupby("user_id")["day"].mean().reset_index()["day"]
    result = pd.DataFrame({
        "user_id": df["user_id"].unique(),
        "user_converted": user_converted,
        "user_treatment": user_treatment,
        "user_platform": user_platform,
        "user_day_mean": user_day_mean,
    })
    return result

options.label: OLS linear regression
options.rationale: Fit an ordinary least squares model with user_converted as the outcome to estimate the absolute probability lift (treatment - control) in percentage points.
options.spec: Fit an OLS regression (statsmodels.api.OLS) of user_converted on user_treatment (dummy coded: treatment=1, control=0) and covariates indicated by ctx['covariates'] (with platform dropped first if present). Use HC1 (heteroskedasticity-consistent) standard errors. Return the coefficient for user_treatment as estimate (in percentage points, so multiply by 100), its 95% CI, and p-value.
options.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm


def estimate(df, ctx):
    names = [] + [str(c) for c in ctx.get('covariates', [])]
    names = [c for c in dict.fromkeys(names) if c not in ['user_converted', 'user_treatment']]
    used = list(dict.fromkeys(['user_converted', 'user_treatment'] + names))
    data = df.dropna(subset=used)
    finite = [c for c in used if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    data = data[np.isfinite(data[finite].astype(float)).all(axis=1)]
    hit = data['user_treatment'].astype(str) == 'treatment'
    numeric = pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data['user_treatment'])
    binary = numeric and set(pd.unique(data['user_treatment'])) <= {0, 1}
    if numeric and not binary and not (data['user_treatment'] % 1 == 0).all():
        raise ValueError('the exposure is coded 1 only where user_treatment equals treatment exactly, but user_treatment is a numeric column with fractional values, so one value is not a group; to cut it, code 1 for values at or above the cut after dropping the rows where user_treatment is missing')
    if not hit.any() and not binary:
        raise ValueError(
            'the exposure level ' + 'treatment' + ' is not a value of the column ' + 'user_treatment'
        )
    if hit.any():
        data = data.assign(**{'user_treatment': hit.astype(float)})
    if len(data) and data['user_treatment'].nunique() < 2:
        raise ValueError('the exposure ' + 'user_treatment' + ' has the same value in every row, so it is collinear with the intercept and its effect cannot be estimated: the earlier step that builds it produced a constant. A threshold taken from a numpy median, percentile or quantile is NaN when the column has missing values, and no row then passes it. The pandas median and quantile methods skip missing values')
    core = data[['user_treatment']].astype(float)
    parts = [core]
    numeric = [c for c in names if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    other = [c for c in names if c not in numeric]
    if numeric:
        parts.append(data[numeric].astype(float))
    if other:
        dummies = pd.get_dummies(data[other].astype(str), drop_first=True, dtype=float)
        parts.append(dummies)
    exog = sm.add_constant(pd.concat(parts, axis=1), has_constant='add')
    labels = pd.Series(exog.columns.map(str))
    repeats = labels.groupby(labels).cumcount()
    exog.columns = [f'{c}_repeat{n}' if n else c for c, n in zip(labels, repeats)]
    protected = ['const', *map(str, core.columns)]
    basis = np.zeros((len(exog), 0))
    aliased = []
    for column in list(exog.columns):
        vector = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(vector))
        residual = vector / size if size else vector
        for _ in range(2):
            residual = residual - basis @ (basis.T @ residual)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(residual))
        if size >= 1e-07:
            basis = np.column_stack([basis, residual / size])
        elif str(column) not in protected:
            aliased.append(str(column))
    kept = [c for c in exog.columns if c not in aliased]
    tangled = []
    for column in aliased:
        target = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        weights = np.linalg.lstsq(exog[kept].to_numpy(dtype=float), target, rcond=None)[0]
        sizes = np.abs(weights) * exog[kept].abs().max().to_numpy(dtype=float)
        floor = 1e-07 * (float(np.abs(target).max()) or 1.0)
        involved = [c for c, size in zip(kept, sizes) if size > floor]
        if any(c in core.columns for c in involved):
            tangled += [c for c in involved if c not in protected]
    tangled = list(dict.fromkeys(tangled))
    exog = exog.drop(columns=aliased + tangled)
    note = 'aliased covariates dropped: ' + ', '.join(aliased) if aliased else ''
    note += '; covariates that rebuild the exposure with them dropped: ' + ', '.join(tangled) if tangled else ''
    endog = data['user_converted'].astype(float)
    model = sm.OLS(endog, exog)
    fit = model.fit(cov_type="HC1")
    term = 'user_treatment'
    ci = fit.conf_int()
    low, high = (float(v) for v in ci.loc[term])
    value = float(fit.params[term])
    p_value = float(fit.pvalues[term])
    return {
        "estimate": value,
        "ci_low": low,
        "ci_high": high,
        "p_value": p_value,
        "n": int(len(data)),
        "note": note,
    }

steps.title: Aggregate to user-level
steps.description: Aggregate session-level data to user-level since variant is assigned per user, computing user conversion (any session converted) and averaging platform/day covariates.

options.label: User converted if any session converted
options.rationale: Define user-level conversion as 1 if any of their sessions resulted in a purchase, reflecting user-level decision.
options.spec: Group by user_id. For each user: compute user_converted = max(converted) across sessions; user_treatment = variant of first session (all same per user); user_platform = mode of platform; user_day_mean = mean of day; return dataframe with one row per user and columns: user_id, user_converted, user_treatment, user_platform, user_day_mean.
options.code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def apply(df, ctx):
    # user_converted: 1 if any session converted
    user_converted = df.groupby("user_id")["converted"].max().reset_index()["converted"]
    # user_treatment: variant of first session (all same per user)
    user_treatment = df.groupby("user_id")["variant"].first().reset_index()["variant"]
    # user_platform: mode of platform per user
    user_platform = df.groupby("user_id")["platform"].apply(lambda x: x.mode().iloc[0] if not x.mode().empty else np.nan).reset_index()["platform"]
    # user_day_mean: mean of day per user
    user_day_mean = df.groupby("user_id")["day"].mean().reset_index()["day"]
    result = pd.DataFrame({
        "user_id": df["user_id"].unique(),
        "user_converted": user_converted,
        "user_treatment": user_treatment,
        "user_platform": user_platform,
        "user_day_mean": user_day_mean,
    })
    return result

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm


def estimate(df, ctx):
    names = [] + [str(c) for c in ctx.get('covariates', [])]
    names = [c for c in dict.fromkeys(names) if c not in ['user_converted', 'user_treatment']]
    used = list(dict.fromkeys(['user_converted', 'user_treatment'] + names))
    data = df.dropna(subset=used)
    finite = [c for c in used if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    data = data[np.isfinite(data[finite].astype(float)).all(axis=1)]
    hit = data['user_treatment'].astype(str) == 'treatment'
    numeric = pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data['user_treatment'])
    binary = numeric and set(pd.unique(data['user_treatment'])) <= {0, 1}
    if numeric and not binary and not (data['user_treatment'] % 1 == 0).all():
        raise ValueError('the exposure is coded 1 only where user_treatment equals treatment exactly, but user_treatment is a numeric column with fractional values, so one value is not a group; to cut it, code 1 for values at or above the cut after dropping the rows where user_treatment is missing')
    if not hit.any() and not binary:
        raise ValueError(
            'the exposure level ' + 'treatment' + ' is not a value of the column ' + 'user_treatment'
        )
    if hit.any():
        data = data.assign(**{'user_treatment': hit.astype(float)})
    if len(data) and data['user_treatment'].nunique() < 2:
        raise ValueError('the exposure ' + 'user_treatment' + ' has the same value in every row, so it is collinear with the intercept and its effect cannot be estimated: the earlier step that builds it produced a constant. A threshold taken from a numpy median, percentile or quantile is NaN when the column has missing values, and no row then passes it. The pandas median and quantile methods skip missing values')
    core = data[['user_treatment']].astype(float)
    parts = [core]
    numeric = [c for c in names if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    other = [c for c in names if c not in numeric]
    if numeric:
        parts.append(data[numeric].astype(float))
    if other:
        dummies = pd.get_dummies(data[other].astype(str), drop_first=True, dtype=float)
        parts.append(dummies)
    exog = sm.add_constant(pd.concat(parts, axis=1), has_constant='add')
    labels = pd.Series(exog.columns.map(str))
    repeats = labels.groupby(labels).cumcount()
    exog.columns = [f'{c}_repeat{n}' if n else c for c, n in zip(labels, repeats)]
    protected = ['const', *map(str, core.columns)]
    basis = np.zeros((len(exog), 0))
    aliased = []
    for column in list(exog.columns):
        vector = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(vector))
        residual = vector / size if size else vector
        for _ in range(2):
            residual = residual - basis @ (basis.T @ residual)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(residual))
        if size >= 1e-07:
            basis = np.column_stack([basis, residual / size])
        elif str(column) not in protected:
            aliased.append(str(column))
    kept = [c for c in exog.columns if c not in aliased]
    tangled = []
    for column in aliased:
        target = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        weights = np.linalg.lstsq(exog[kept].to_numpy(dtype=float), target, rcond=None)[0]
        sizes = np.abs(weights) * exog[kept].abs().max().to_numpy(dtype=float)
        floor = 1e-07 * (float(np.abs(target).max()) or 1.0)
        involved = [c for c, size in zip(kept, sizes) if size > floor]
        if any(c in core.columns for c in involved):
            tangled += [c for c in involved if c not in protected]
    tangled = list(dict.fromkeys(tangled))
    exog = exog.drop(columns=aliased + tangled)
    note = 'aliased covariates dropped: ' + ', '.join(aliased) if aliased else ''
    note += '; covariates that rebuild the exposure with them dropped: ' + ', '.join(tangled) if tangled else ''
    endog = data['user_converted'].astype(float)
    model = sm.OLS(endog, exog)
    fit = model.fit(cov_type="HC1")
    term = 'user_treatment'
    ci = fit.conf_int()
    low, high = (float(v) for v in ci.loc[term])
    value = float(fit.params[term])
    p_value = float(fit.pvalues[term])
    return {
        "estimate": value,
        "ci_low": low,
        "ci_high": high,
        "p_value": p_value,
        "n": int(len(data)),
        "note": note,
    }

        for _ in range(2):
            residual = residual - basis @ (basis.T @ residual)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(residual))
        if size >= 1e-07:
            basis = np.column_stack([basis, residual / size])
        elif str(column) not in protected:
            aliased.append(str(column))
    kept = [c for c in exog.columns if c not in aliased]
    tangled = []
    for column in aliased:
        target = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        weights = np.linalg.lstsq(exog[kept].to_numpy(dtype=float), target, rcond=None)[0]
        sizes = np.abs(weights) * exog[kept].abs().max().to_numpy(dtype=float)
        floor = 1e-07 * (float(np.abs(target).max()) or 1.0)
        involved = [c for c, size in zip(kept, sizes) if size > floor]
        if any(c in core.columns for c in involved):
            tangled += [c for c in involved if c not in protected]
    tangled = list(dict.fromkeys(tangled))
    exog = exog.drop(columns=aliased + tangled)
    note = 'aliased covariates dropped: ' + ', '.join(aliased) if aliased else ''
    note += '; covariates that rebuild the exposure with them dropped: ' + ', '.join(tangled) if tangled else ''
    endog = data['user_converted'].astype(float)
    model = sm.OLS(endog, exog)
    fit = model.fit(cov_type="HC3")
    term = 'user_treatment'
    ci = fit.conf_int()
    low, high = (float(v) for v in ci.loc[term])
    value = float(fit.params[term])
    p_value = float(fit.pvalues[term])
    return {
        "estimate": value,
        "ci_low": low,
        "ci_high": high,
        "p_value": p_value,
        "n": int(len(data)),
        "note": note,
    }

report.narrative: The original analysis estimated 0.849 (95% CI 0.152 to 1.55, p = 0.017, n = 16,000) and returned the verdict SHIP. The minimal flip changes Filter internal/bot-like sessions from "Keep all sessions" to "Exclude internal sessions". This change removes 171 sessions flagged as internal staff or test users (n falls to 15,829) and moves the estimate to -0.149 (95% CI -0.799 to 0.500, p = 0.653), reversing the verdict to DON'T SHIP. The judge accepted this option as defensible (defensibility 0.85) because excluding internal/test sessions improves validity by removing non-customer activity, a common practice in A/B testing. The flip was reproduced by an independent re-execution. Two other accepted options on the same step also reverse the verdict: "Exclude internal and bot-like sessions" (estimate -0.126, p = 0.707, n = 15,564) and combinations that include either internal-session exclusion. The option "Exclude bot-like sessions" alone does not flip (estimate 0.891, p = 0.014). Covariate adjustment choices (unadjusted or platform-and-day) and estimation method (OLS vs logistic) shift the estimate by at most 0.005 and never change the verdict. Robustness: 56% of the analysis grid agrees with the original verdict and 44% reverses it.
caveats: The options 'Keep all sessions' and 'Exclude extremely long sessions' of the step 'Filter internal/bot-like sessions' have different specs but produced identical output on the smoke sample even after one re-code, so one of them may not implement its own spec.
16 universes ran but only 15 gave distinct results; universes with identical results are counted once in the robustness share.

The option 'Exclude extremely long sessions' (filter_records) is a no-op: its step output is identical to the baseline option's (same data fingerprint after the step), so it is not a different analysis. It is excluded from the robustness share and from the flip search.

Robustness headline: 56% of the analysis grid agrees with the original verdict (uniform random sample of the grid: 12 draws (each decision picks each of its options equally), 9 distinct results; independent of the beam search). Among the universes the search explored, 67% agree, but the beam search samples the universes that are closest to flipping, so that share leans toward flips.
